before.content_html:
What is Homeostasis?

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (B3.3a). This matters because enzymes and metabolic reactions work within narrow ranges of temperature, pH, blood glucose and water balance. If any of these drift too far from the optimum, cell processes slow down or stop — potentially with fatal consequences.

All homeostatic systems share the same three-part architecture: receptors detect deviations from the normal level, a coordination centre (such as the brain or pancreas) processes the information and sends instructions, and effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response. The system operates through negative feedback: once conditions return to normal, the response is switched off.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment using negative feedback. Every control system has three components: receptor (detects change), coordination centre (processes information), effector (produces the corrective response).

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored continuously by the pancreas (B3.3b–c). When blood glucose rises after a carbohydrate-rich meal, specialised beta cells in the pancreas detect the increase and release insulin into the blood. Insulin has two effects: it causes body cells (especially muscles and liver) to absorb glucose from the blood, and it stimulates the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen for storage. Both effects lower blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose falls — for example, during exercise or between meals — alpha cells in the pancreas detect the drop and release glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to break glycogen back down into glucose (glycogenolysis) and release it into the blood, raising glucose back to normal. The opposing actions of insulin (lowering glucose) and glucagon (raising glucose) form a classic negative feedback loop that maintains blood glucose within a safe, narrow range (B3.3b, Higher Tier).

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition: the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Without insulin, blood glucose rises dangerously after eating. Treatment requires regular insulin injections (or an insulin pump) combined with careful monitoring of blood glucose and carbohydrate intake. It usually develops in childhood or early adulthood and cannot be prevented (B3.3d).

Type 2 diabetes develops when body cells become resistant to insulin — they no longer respond appropriately, so blood glucose stays elevated even though the pancreas may still produce insulin. It is strongly associated with obesity, a sedentary lifestyle and genetic factors. Treatment typically involves a controlled diet (limiting refined carbohydrates and sugars), regular exercise, and sometimes medication. Type 2 can often be prevented or managed through lifestyle changes, unlike Type 1 (B3.3d).

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: the pancreas cannot produce insulin (autoimmune; treated with insulin injections). Type 2 diabetes: body cells become resistant to insulin (often linked to obesity; treated with diet and exercise, sometimes medication).

Temperature Regulation

Core body temperature in humans is maintained at approximately 37 °C by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain (B3.3c). It receives signals from thermoreceptors in the skin (detecting external temperature) and from receptors monitoring blood temperature in the brain itself. Together these provide a complete picture of the body’s thermal state, allowing the coordination centre to activate appropriate effectors.

When the body is too hot, three main effector responses lower temperature. Vasodilation: blood vessels near the skin surface widen, so more warm blood flows close to the skin and more heat is radiated away. Sweating: sweat glands release sweat onto the skin; water in sweat evaporates, removing heat energy from the skin (evaporative cooling). Body hairs lying flat: erector muscles relax, so hairs lie flat against the skin, reducing the insulating layer of trapped air.

Vasoconstriction: blood vessels near the skin surface narrow, diverting blood away from the skin and reducing heat loss by radiation. Shivering: skeletal muscles contract rapidly and repeatedly; the increased metabolic activity generates heat that warms the body. Body hairs standing on end: erector muscles contract, raising hairs and trapping a thicker insulating layer of air close to the skin (more effective in furry animals than in humans).

Both sets of responses illustrate negative feedback — once body temperature returns to 37 °C, the thermoreceptors detect the change and the effector responses are switched off. This cyclical on-off control is what keeps core temperature within a narrow, safe range.

It is worth noting that the nervous and endocrine systems work together in thermoregulation. The nervous system sends rapid signals to sweat glands and erector muscles (which raise body hairs), while hormones such as adrenaline can also boost metabolic heat production in emergency cold exposure. The skin acts as the primary interface with the environment — its rich blood supply and large surface area make it the key organ for heat exchange. Evaporative cooling via sweat is particularly important during physical exercise, when the body can generate large amounts of metabolic heat through increased muscle respiration.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vasoconstriction helps the body conserve heat when core temperature drops.

practice_questions.text: A student measures their blood glucose at four time points: fasting (5.0 mmol/L), 30 min after a meal (8.4 mmol/L), 60 min after a meal (6.9 mmol/L) and 120 min after a meal (5.1 mmol/L). Calculate the percentage decrease in blood glucose between 30 min and 120 min. Show your working and give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decrease = 8.4 − 5.1 = 3.3 mmol/L (1); percentage decrease = (3.3 ÷ 8.4) × 100 (1) = 39.28...% (1); rounded correctly to 39.3% (1). Penalise missing % symbol or incorrect rounding. Secure: Correct method with arithmetic error in one step (max 3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a person with Type 1 diabetes requires insulin injections but a person with Type 2 diabetes may be able to manage their condition without injections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: In Type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells so no insulin is produced; without injections, blood glucose cannot be controlled (1). In Type 2 diabetes, the pancreas may still produce insulin but body cells are resistant to it (1); lifestyle changes such as diet and exercise can reduce insulin resistance and improve glucose uptake without the need for injections (1). Secure: Two of the three points. Developing: Distinguishes the two types but does not explain why injections are only needed in Type 1. Emerging: Confuses the two types.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of negative feedback in maintaining blood glucose homeostasis. In your answer, explain what would happen if negative feedback mechanisms failed, with reference to diabetes as an example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Negative feedback ensures that any deviation from the set point (normal blood glucose) triggers a corrective response that brings glucose back to normal — preventing it from rising too high (hyperglycaemia) or falling too low (hypoglycaemia), both of which are dangerous. Without insulin (as in Type 1 diabetes), blood glucose can rise after eating and cells are deprived of glucose for respiration, leading to fatigue, organ damage and, if untreated, diabetic ketoacidosis. Without glucagon (Higher Tier), blood glucose could fall dangerously, impairing brain function since the brain relies almost entirely on glucose. The fact that two opposing hormones (insulin and glucagon) are involved makes the system more responsive and precise than a single-hormone system. A clear evaluative conclusion on why negative feedback is essential for survival. Secure: Four well-made points. Developing: Two points, limited evaluation. Emerging: One relevant point.

before.content_html:
The Role of the Kidneys

The kidneys are a pair of organs responsible for two key homeostatic functions: excretion (removing metabolic waste, especially urea from protein breakdown) and osmoregulation (controlling the water and ion concentration of the blood) (B3.3e). They filter the blood continuously, retaining useful substances and excreting waste products as urine.

Blood is delivered to each kidney via the renal artery (bringing blood to the kidney) and leaves via the renal vein (carrying cleaned blood away from the kidney). Urine drains from the kidney via the ureter to the bladder, and is expelled via the urethra. A common exam error is stating that the artery takes blood away — remember: arteries arrive at the organ.

Key Fact

The renal artery delivers blood to the kidney; the renal vein carries filtered blood away. Urine drains through the ureter to the bladder and out via the urethra.

How the Kidney Filters Blood

The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron. Blood enters the nephron at the glomerulus — a knot of capillaries inside a cup-shaped structure called the Bowman’s capsule. The high blood pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules out of the blood and into the Bowman’s capsule — this is ultrafiltration. Molecules that pass through include water, glucose, urea and mineral ions. Large molecules (proteins and red blood cells) are too big to pass through and remain in the blood.

The fluid now in the tubule (the filtrate) is not yet urine — it contains useful substances that must be recovered. As the filtrate travels along the tubule, selective reabsorption returns all glucose (via active transport), most water, and the required amount of mineral ions back into the surrounding capillaries. What remains — water, urea and excess ions — passes on to become urine (B3.3e).

A student analyses the filtrate in the Bowman’s capsule and the urine. They find glucose in the filtrate but not in the urine. Explain why.

Step 1: Glucose is a small molecule, so it passes through the glomerulus into the filtrate during ultrafiltration. Step 2: As the filtrate passes through the tubule, all glucose is selectively reabsorbed via active transport back into the capillaries. Step 3: Therefore, no glucose remains in the fluid that becomes urine. Note: If glucose were found in urine, this would suggest diabetes — blood glucose is so high that the kidneys cannot reabsorb all of it.

Water Balance and ADH

The amount of water reabsorbed in the kidney is regulated by the hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone) (B3.3f). ADH is produced in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary gland. It acts on the collecting ducts and distal tubule of the nephron, making them more permeable to water so that more water is reabsorbed back into the blood.

When the blood is too concentrated (e.g. after sweating or not drinking enough), osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the increase. More ADH is released → kidney tubules become more permeable → more water is reabsorbed → small volumes of concentrated (dark) urine are produced. Blood water content returns to normal.

When blood is too dilute (e.g. after drinking a lot of water), osmoreceptors detect the decrease in concentration. Less ADH is released → kidney tubules become less permeable → less water is reabsorbed → large volumes of dilute (pale) urine are produced. This is a classic negative feedback loop: the output (water reabsorption and urine concentration) reverses the original change (blood concentration).

Key Fact

ADH controls water reabsorption in the kidney. High blood concentration → more ADH → concentrated urine. Low blood concentration → less ADH → dilute urine. This is negative feedback control of water balance (osmoregulation).

Kidney Failure and Treatments

If the kidneys fail, toxic waste products (especially urea) and excess water build up in the blood. Without treatment, this is fatal. Two main treatments exist for kidney failure (B3.3g): dialysis and kidney transplantation.

In haemodialysis, the patient’s blood is passed through a machine containing a partially permeable membrane. On the other side of the membrane is dialysis fluid, which has the same concentration of useful substances (glucose, mineral ions) as normal blood but contains no urea. Urea and excess ions diffuse from the blood through the membrane into the dialysis fluid, which is discarded. The cleaned blood is returned to the patient.

Dialysis must be performed regularly (typically three times per week, each session lasting several hours). It maintains life but does not cure kidney failure. Patients must follow a careful diet to manage urea build-up between sessions. It is a significant commitment and can affect quality of life.

A kidney transplant replaces the failed organ with a healthy one from a compatible donor (living or recently deceased). If successful, the transplanted kidney functions normally and the patient no longer needs dialysis. Donors with closely matched tissue types (determined by surface antigens on cells) are preferable because they reduce the risk of the immune system rejecting the new organ.

To prevent rejection, patients must take immunosuppressant drugs for the rest of their lives. These reduce immune system activity, preventing rejection — but they also make the patient more vulnerable to infection. Despite these disadvantages, a successful transplant typically offers a better quality of life than long-term dialysis. The main limiting factor is the availability of suitable donor kidneys.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: High blood pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules (water, glucose, urea, mineral ions) out of the blood and through the capillary walls into the Bowman's capsule to form the filtrate (1); large molecules such as proteins and blood cells are too big to pass through and remain in the blood (1). practice_questions.text: Explain how ADH brings about a change in urine concentration when a person becomes dehydrated.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: When blood becomes more concentrated (dehydration), osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this (1); more ADH is released from the pituitary gland (1); ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood, producing a small volume of concentrated urine (1). Secure: Two points correctly linked. Developing: States 'ADH causes concentrated urine' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: No mechanistic detail.

practice_questions.text: A dialysis patient's blood urea concentration is measured before and after a dialysis session. Before: 28 mmol/L. After: 6 mmol/L. Calculate the percentage decrease in urea concentration. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Decrease = 28 − 6 = 22 mmol/L (1); percentage decrease = (22 ÷ 28) × 100 (1) = 78.57...% (1); rounded to 78.6% (1). Penalise missing % sign or incorrect rounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why dialysis fluid contains glucose but no urea.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood (1); this prevents glucose from diffusing out of the blood across the partially permeable membrane, so the patient does not lose glucose (1); the fluid contains no urea, so urea diffuses from the blood (higher concentration) into the dialysis fluid (lower concentration) down the concentration gradient, removing it from the blood (1). Secure: Two of the three points. Developing: States 'so glucose is not lost' and 'urea moves out' with no reference to concentration gradients. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of a kidney transplant compared to long-term dialysis for a patient with kidney failure.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Transplant advantages — kidney functions normally, so the patient no longer needs time-consuming dialysis sessions; quality of life is typically much better; no ongoing cost per session; can eat a more normal diet. Transplant disadvantages — immunosuppressant drugs must be taken for life, increasing infection risk; the operation itself carries surgical risk; suitable donors are scarce. Dialysis advantages — widely available; no surgery required; does not rely on a donor. Dialysis disadvantages — requires sessions several times per week, each lasting several hours; dietary restrictions must be maintained; long-term quality of life is generally lower. A justified conclusion that weighs both sides, noting that a successful transplant is generally preferred but is limited by donor availability and rejection risk. Secure: Four points with some evaluation. Developing: Two advantages and one disadvantage with limited evaluation. Emerging: One point.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The kidneys filter blood through ultrafiltration (small molecules into the filtrate) then selectively reabsorb glucose, useful ions and water. The renal artery brings blood to the kidney; the renal vein carries it away.
  • ADH controls water reabsorption via negative feedback: high blood concentration → more ADH → concentrated urine; low blood concentration → less ADH → dilute urine.
  • Kidney failure is treated by dialysis (regular blood filtration through a partially permeable membrane) or kidney transplant (better quality of life but requires immunosuppressant drugs and a compatible donor).

before.content_html:
Levels of Organisation in an Ecosystem

An ecosystem is a community of organisms interacting with one another and with the abiotic (non-living) environment they share (B4.1d). All ecosystems are built from the same hierarchy of levels: individual organisms of the same species form a population, different populations living together form a community, and a community plus its abiotic environment makes an ecosystem.

Within communities, organisms are linked by interdependence (B4.1f). Organisms compete for limited resources: animals compete for food, water, territory and mates; plants compete for light, water, mineral ions and space. Relationships also include predation (one organism hunts and eats another), mutualism (both species benefit, as when bees collect nectar while pollinating flowers) and parasitism (one species benefits while harming the other, as in a tapeworm in a host’s gut).

Key Fact

Ecosystems are organised as: organism → population (one species) → community (many species) → ecosystem (community + abiotic environment). Organisms are interdependent through predation, mutualism, parasitism and competition.

Biotic and Abiotic Factors

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that shape an ecosystem: temperature, light intensity, moisture level, soil pH, wind speed, and dissolved oxygen in aquatic habitats. Biotic factors are living components: predator numbers, disease prevalence, food availability and competition with other species (B4.1e). Changes in either type affect the size and distribution of populations throughout the community.

A classic example of biotic interaction is the predator–prey cycle. In a stable ecosystem, predator and prey populations oscillate: as prey numbers increase (abundant food), predator numbers rise; increased predation reduces prey numbers; with less food, predator numbers fall; prey then recover. This negative feedback keeps both populations within bounds. If an abiotic factor such as drought also reduces prey, the predator population decline is amplified.

Scientists use indicator species to monitor ecosystem health. Lichens are indicators of air quality — they are highly sensitive to sulfur dioxide pollution and disappear from areas with poor air quality. Freshwater invertebrates such as stonefly larvae (intolerant of pollution) or blood worms (tolerant of low oxygen) indicate the degree of water pollution. Monitoring these species provides an early warning of environmental change (B4.1e).

Food Chains, Webs and Trophic Levels

Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, captured by producers through photosynthesis. Energy then passes through trophic levels (B4.1a–b): producer → primary consumer (herbivore) → secondary consumer (carnivore) → tertiary consumer (top predator). A food web shows all the interconnected food chains in a community and illustrates how changes to one population ripple through the whole system.

In a simple terrestrial food chain: grass → rabbit → fox → eagle. Grass is the producer; the rabbit is the primary consumer (herbivore); the fox is the secondary consumer (omnivore/carnivore); the eagle is the tertiary consumer (top predator). Removing the fox from this web allows rabbit numbers to increase, which in turn over-grazes the grass, eventually reducing plant cover.

Food webs are more realistic than single food chains because most consumers eat more than one type of food. This interconnectedness gives ecosystems a degree of resilience — if one prey species declines, a predator may switch to an alternative. However, highly complex food webs can still collapse if a key species at a lower trophic level is lost.

Energy Transfer and Efficiency

At each trophic level, energy is transferred to the next level but a large proportion is lost to the surroundings — through respiration (heat), movement and waste products (faeces, urine). As a result, the biomass available at each successive trophic level is considerably less than at the level below. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels: there is simply not enough energy left to support another level.

The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is typically around 10% (the “10% rule”), though this varies with species and conditions. If producers capture 10,000 kJ of energy from sunlight, only approximately 1,000 kJ is available to primary consumers, around 100 kJ to secondary consumers, and only about 10 kJ to tertiary consumers. This helps explain why eating lower on the food chain (e.g. eating plant-based foods rather than meat) is more energy-efficient from a global food security perspective (B4.1c, Higher Tier).

A pyramid of biomass represents the total mass of organisms at each trophic level at a given moment. Unlike pyramids of numbers (which can be inverted — a single oak tree supporting thousands of insects), biomass pyramids are almost always true pyramids: each bar is smaller than the one below because energy and therefore mass decrease at each trophic level.

To construct a biomass pyramid, weigh (or estimate) all organisms at each trophic level in the same area and time period. The bars should be drawn to scale (area or length proportional to biomass). Biomass is usually expressed in grams or kilograms per unit area (g/m2 or kg/m2). A key limitation of a snapshot pyramid is that it does not account for the fact that producers (e.g. algae) reproduce quickly — a small total algal biomass may support a large fish population if turnover is rapid.

Key Fact

Energy (and therefore biomass) decreases at each trophic level because energy is lost through respiration, movement and waste. This is why pyramids of biomass narrow at each level and food chains rarely exceed four or five links.

Adaptations and Biodiversity

Organisms have adaptations — inherited features that improve survival and reproduction in their environment (B4.1d). These may be structural (e.g. a polar bear’s thick fur and subcutaneous fat for insulation), behavioural (e.g. nocturnal hunting to avoid daytime predators) or functional (e.g. a camel’s ability to concentrate urine to conserve water). Adaptations arise over many generations through natural selection and shape which organisms live in a given ecosystem.

Biodiversity refers to the variety of species present. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more resilient: if one species declines, others can partially fill its role. Human activities such as deforestation, intensive farming, pollution and over-hunting reduce biodiversity. Conservation programmes — protected habitats, captive breeding, seed banks — aim to preserve biodiversity for ecological stability and future generations.
before.exam_tip_html: For food web questions that ask you to predict what happens if one species is removed, always trace the effect up and down the web — a decline in prey affects predators; an increase in prey affects the trophic level below. For energy transfer questions, make sure you state that energy is lost as heat through respiration — not simply ‘lost’. For abiotic vs biotic factor questions, use clear examples: temperature (abiotic) vs competition for food (biotic). Higher Tier calculations of energy transfer percentage require you to divide the energy at one trophic level by the energy at the level below, then multiply by 100.

before.content_html:
Sexual and Asexual Reproduction

There are two fundamentally different ways organisms reproduce. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes (sperm and egg). Because each gamete carries a different mix of genetic material, the offspring are genetically varied from each other and from both parents. This variation is the raw material for natural selection (B5.1a).

Asexual reproduction involves a single parent. No gametes are formed or fused. Cell division by mitosis produces offspring that are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Bacteria, some plants (e.g. strawberry runners) and some animals (e.g. hydra) can reproduce asexually. The advantage is speed and efficiency: no mate is required. The disadvantage is that all offspring are identical, so if the environment changes or disease strikes, all may be equally vulnerable.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction: two parents, gametes fuse, offspring are genetically varied (benefits natural selection). Asexual reproduction: one parent, mitosis only, offspring are clones (benefits rapid colonisation in stable environments).

Meiosis

Meiosis is the cell division that produces gametes (B5.1b). It occurs in the ovaries and testes. Before meiosis begins, the DNA is replicated. The cell then undergoes two rounds of division:

First division: homologous chromosome pairs line up and then separate into two cells — each cell now has one chromosome from each pair. Second division: each of those cells divides again, producing four cells in total. Each of the four cells is haploid (containing half the normal chromosome number — 23 chromosomes in humans rather than 46). Crucially, genetic material is shuffled during the first division (a process called crossing over), so all four cells are genetically different from each other and from the parent cell.

When two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full chromosome number is restored: the fertilised egg (zygote) contains 46 chromosomes in humans (23 from each gamete). The zygote then divides by mitosis to form the embryo.

Mitosis: one division → 2 cells produced → diploid (full chromosome number) → genetically identical to parent → used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

Meiosis: two divisions → 4 cells produced → haploid (half chromosome number) → genetically different from each other and from parent → used to produce gametes for sexual reproduction. Both start with DNA replication, but only meiosis shuffles genetic material to create variation.

DNA Structure

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made of two strands wound around each other in a double helix. DNA is found in the nucleus of cells, packaged into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs (B5.1c).

Each strand of DNA is made of repeating units called nucleotides. Every nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). The two strands are held together by complementary base pairs: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. This complementary base pairing is fundamental to both DNA replication and protein synthesis.

A gene is a specific section of DNA on a chromosome. The sequence of bases along a gene provides a code that determines the order in which amino acids are assembled to build a protein. Different base sequences produce different proteins, and it is proteins — as enzymes, hormones and structural components — that ultimately determine most of the characteristics of an organism.

Key Fact

DNA is a polymer forming a double helix, held together by complementary base pairs (A–T and C–G). A gene is a section of DNA coding for a specific protein. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. The base sequence determines which protein is made.

Protein Synthesis

Protein synthesis involves two linked stages: transcription (in the nucleus) and translation (at the ribosomes in the cytoplasm) (B5.1c, Separate-only depth).

Transcription: The relevant section of DNA is unwound and one strand (the template strand) is used as a template. Free RNA nucleotides align with their complementary bases on the template strand to build a single-stranded molecule of mRNA (messenger RNA). Note that in RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T), so A on DNA pairs with U on mRNA. The mRNA strand then leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores and moves to the cytoplasm.

Translation: At the ribosomes, the mRNA code is read in groups of three bases (codons). Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids to the ribosome, matching their anticodon to the corresponding mRNA codon. The ribosome joins the amino acids together in the correct sequence to form a polypeptide chain. The chain folds into a specific three-dimensional shape to produce a functional protein. Different amino acid sequences produce proteins with different shapes and functions.

The genetic variation produced by meiosis (through chromosome shuffling and crossing over) and by fertilisation (random combination of gametes) means that offspring in sexually reproducing species are never genetically identical (unless they are identical twins). This variation provides the raw material for natural selection: individuals with alleles that better suit a changing environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those alleles to the next generation. Without variation, a species cannot adapt to environmental change.

knowledge_checks.q: How many cells does meiosis produce, and what is their chromosome number compared to the parent cell?
Which base in RNA replaces thymine (T) and pairs with adenine (A) on the DNA template strand?
The fusion of male and female gametes during sexual reproduction is called _____.
During transcription, the _____ strand of DNA is used as a template to build a complementary mRNA molecule.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: A single-stranded molecule that carries the genetic code from the nucleus to the ribosomes
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A structure in the nucleus made of tightly coiled DNA carrying many genes

practice_questions.text: State how many chromosomes are found in a human gamete.
Describe two ways in which meiosis produces genetically different cells.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Chromosomes are shuffled during the first division (independent assortment) so different combinations of chromosomes enter each new cell (1); crossing over (exchange of sections between homologous chromosomes) produces new combinations of alleles within each chromosome (1). Secure: Two valid points, may use simpler language. Developing: States 'the cells are all different' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: One point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the sequence of bases in a gene determines the characteristics of an organism.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The base sequence of a gene determines the sequence of amino acids assembled during protein synthesis (1); amino acid sequence determines the shape and therefore the function of the protein produced (1); proteins include enzymes, hormones and structural components that ultimately control the characteristics (phenotype) of the organism (1). Secure: Two points clearly linked. Developing: States 'genes code for proteins which control characteristics' without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: Vague or circular definition.

practice_questions.text: A section of DNA template strand has the base sequence: T-A-C-G-G-A. Write the complementary mRNA sequence that would be produced during transcription. Remember that uracil (U) replaces thymine in RNA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A-U-G-C-C-U (1 mark per correct pair, up to 3 marks); all six bases correctly identified = 3 marks; correct use of U instead of T in mRNA (1 additional mark for no T appearing in the mRNA sequence). Total: 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why sexual reproduction produces offspring with greater variation than asexual reproduction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: In sexual reproduction, meiosis shuffles chromosomes during gamete formation, producing gametes with unique combinations of alleles (1); fertilisation combines gametes from two parents, further increasing genetic diversity (1); asexual reproduction uses mitosis, producing offspring with identical genetic material to the parent (clones), so no new variation is generated (1). Secure: Two points. Developing: States 'sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents' without explaining meiosis or fertilisation. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of translation and explain how it produces a functional protein from the mRNA code.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The mRNA strand produced during transcription moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and attaches to a ribosome. The ribosome reads the mRNA code in triplets (codons). Each codon corresponds to a specific amino acid. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids; the anticodon on each tRNA is complementary to the mRNA codon, so the correct amino acid is brought to the ribosome. The ribosome catalyses the formation of peptide bonds between successive amino acids, building a growing polypeptide chain. When a stop codon is reached, the chain is released and folds into a specific three-dimensional shape determined by its amino acid sequence. This shape determines the protein's function (e.g. active site of an enzyme). A well-structured answer that connects each step clearly. Secure: Four steps described. Developing: Mentions ribosomes and amino acids but misses tRNA or codon/anticodon. Emerging: One or two steps with no mechanism.

before.content_html:
Why Monitor Ecosystems?

Scientists monitor the distribution and abundance of organisms to understand the health of ecosystems and detect the effects of human activity or environmental change. Field investigations use sampling techniques to estimate population sizes without counting every individual — a practical necessity when populations are too large or too mobile to census directly. This type of fieldwork is a key skill in biology practical work (PAG B2).

Sampling Techniques

Random sampling uses quadrats placed at coordinates generated randomly (e.g. using a random number table) to avoid bias. The researcher has no influence over where quadrats land. This is suitable for slow-moving or stationary organisms such as plants, limpets or ground-dwelling invertebrates. Results from multiple quadrats are averaged and scaled up to estimate total population size.

Transect sampling places quadrats or records organisms at regular intervals along a line called a transect. This is used to investigate how species distribution changes across a habitat in response to changing abiotic conditions — for example, from the low shore to the high shore of a rocky beach, or from open grassland into a woodland. A belt transect records all organisms within a strip on either side of the line; a line transect records only organisms touching the line.

Key Fact

Random quadrat sampling avoids bias and suits stationary organisms. Transect sampling shows how species distribution changes across a habitat in response to abiotic gradients. Capture-recapture estimates mobile animal populations.

Capture-Recapture and the Lincoln Index

Mobile animals cannot be counted using quadrats. The capture-recapture method involves catching a sample of animals, marking them (e.g. with paint, tags or notches), releasing them, and later catching a second sample. The proportion of marked individuals in the second sample allows the total population size to be estimated using the Lincoln Index:

$$N = \frac{n_1 \times n_2}{m_2}$$

Where \(N\) = estimated population size, \(n_1\) = number in first sample, \(n_2\) = number in second sample, \(m_2\) = number of marked individuals in the second sample.

For example: 40 woodlice are caught, marked and released (\(n_1 = 40\)). The next day, 35 are caught (\(n_2 = 35\)), of which 7 are marked (\(m_2 = 7\)).

$$N = \frac{40 \times 35}{7} = \frac{1400}{7} = 200$$

The estimated population is 200 woodlice. The accuracy of this estimate depends on several assumptions: marked individuals must mix randomly back into the population; marking must not affect survival, behaviour or attractiveness to predators; the population must be closed (no significant births, deaths, immigration or emigration) between the two samples. If these assumptions are violated, the estimate will be unreliable.

Indicator species reveal pollution levels without expensive instruments. Lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide in the air: bushy, leafy lichens grow only in clean air, while crusty lichens tolerate some pollution. Their absence indicates heavily polluted air. Freshwater invertebrates indicate water quality. Stonefly nymphs and freshwater shrimps require clean, well-oxygenated water; their presence indicates low pollution. In contrast, bloodworms (Chironomus larvae) and rat-tailed maggots tolerate low-oxygen, polluted water. A healthy, diverse community of invertebrates suggests good water quality.

Scientists also take direct physical measurements to confirm what indicator species suggest: dissolved oxygen meters, pH probes and nitrate test kits provide quantitative data. Combining biological and physical indicators gives a fuller picture of ecosystem health.

Biodiversity and Human Impact

Biodiversity refers to the variety of living organisms in an area. High biodiversity indicates a healthy, stable ecosystem with many different species filling different ecological roles. Human activities reduce biodiversity through deforestation (habitat loss), pollution, over-exploitation of species and the introduction of invasive non-native species that outcompete native ones.

Eutrophication is a serious consequence of agricultural pollution. When excess nitrate or phosphate fertilisers wash into rivers and lakes, they trigger rapid algal growth (an algal bloom). Dense algae block sunlight, killing aquatic plants below. When algae die, decomposing bacteria multiply and consume dissolved oxygen. Oxygen levels fall so low that fish and other aerobic organisms suffocate. This sequence — nutrient enrichment, algal bloom, light blocking, decomposition, oxygen depletion — is a common extended-response question.

Sustainability requires managing ecosystems so that human use does not exceed natural recovery rates. Conservation strategies include:

• Protected areas — national parks and nature reserves limit harmful human activity.
• Captive breeding programmes — endangered species are bred in captivity with plans for reintroduction to the wild.
• Seed banks — storing seeds from rare plant species as insurance against extinction.
• Fishing quotas and logging regulations — controlling extraction rates to allow populations to recover.
• Reforestation — planting trees to restore habitats and sequester carbon dioxide.

Effective conservation requires long-term monitoring data to determine whether strategies are working, and cooperation between governments, local communities and scientists.

Key Fact

Eutrophication sequence: fertiliser run-off → algal bloom → light blocked (aquatic plants die) → algae die → decomposers multiply → oxygen depleted → aerobic organisms suffocate.

lessons.title: Feeding the Human Race: Selective Breeding and GM

before.content_html:
The Challenge of Food Security

Food security means ensuring that all people have reliable access to sufficient, nutritious food. With the global population growing rapidly, achieving food security is one of the most pressing challenges biologists and agricultural scientists face. Key threats include: population growth (more people need more food), climate change (droughts, floods and extreme weather damage crops), rising costs (fuel and fertiliser price increases raise food prices), conflict (war disrupts farming and distribution) and water scarcity (unreliable irrigation).

Key Fact

Food security is threatened by population growth, climate change, rising costs, conflict and water scarcity. Biologists develop scientific solutions to increase food production sustainably.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with the most desirable characteristics and breed them together over many generations. Over time, the frequency of the desired alleles increases in the population. Examples include:

• Breeding cattle that produce greater quantities of milk or have faster growth rates.
• Developing wheat varieties resistant to fungal diseases such as wheat rust.
• Selecting dogs with specific temperaments and physical traits for different working roles.
• Breeding crop plants with increased yield per hectare.

Selective breeding is effective but has a key limitation: it reduces genetic diversity within the population. Repeated breeding from a small gene pool makes populations more uniform. This means a new pathogen or environmental change to which they have no resistance could devastate the entire population. Selective breeding can also cause health issues in animals when extreme traits are selected (e.g. breathing difficulties in flat-faced dog breeds).

Genetic modification (GM) involves inserting a gene from one organism directly into the DNA of another to give it a new characteristic. Unlike selective breeding, GM can introduce entirely new characteristics from a different species in a single generation. The process involves: identifying the desired gene in a donor organism; cutting it out using restriction enzymes; inserting it into the target organism’s DNA using a vector (often a bacterium or a virus).

GM crops have been engineered to be resistant to insect pests (reducing the need for insecticides), resistant to herbicides (allowing weeds to be killed without harming the crop), tolerant to drought conditions, or capable of producing greater yields. One widely discussed example is golden rice, which has been modified to produce beta-carotene (a precursor to vitamin A) — potentially addressing vitamin A deficiency in populations where rice is a staple food.

Concerns about GM crops include: the possibility that GM genes could spread to wild plant relatives through cross-pollination, creating herbicide-resistant ‘superweeds’; potential unknown long-term effects on human health or ecosystems; ethical objections to interfering with natural genetic sequences; and the concentration of seed ownership in the hands of large corporations, which may disadvantage smallholder farmers.

Key Fact

GM crops can be pest-resistant, drought-tolerant or more nutritious. Concerns include gene transfer to wild plants, unknown long-term effects and ethical objections. Selective breeding reduces genetic diversity over time; GM can introduce new traits in one generation.

Tissue Culture

Tissue culture is a technique used to propagate plants rapidly by taking small samples of plant tissue (called explants), sterilising them and growing them on a nutrient medium containing the correct balance of plant growth hormones. Each explant develops into a complete, whole plant that is genetically identical to the parent plant. This allows large numbers of plants to be produced quickly and reliably from a single parent — useful for preserving rare or endangered plant species, for multiplying commercially high-value varieties such as orchids, and for producing disease-free planting stock. Because all the plants produced are clones, they share the same genetic advantages as the selected parent — but also the same vulnerabilities. If a disease emerges that one plant cannot resist, none of the clones will be resistant either.

Biological control uses living organisms instead of chemical pesticides to manage pests. Examples include introducing ladybirds to feed on aphid colonies on crop plants, or using parasitic wasps that lay eggs inside caterpillars, whose larvae then kill the host. Biological control avoids chemical pollution and is self-sustaining once established, but it can be unpredictable — the introduced organism may become invasive itself, attack non-target species or fail to control the pest effectively.

Integrated pest management (IPM) combines chemical and biological approaches, using pesticides only when pest numbers exceed a threshold and relying on natural predators where possible. This minimises chemical use and environmental impact while protecting crop yields.

Sustainable farming practices that help with food security include crop rotation (alternating crops each season to prevent soil mineral depletion and reduce pest build-up), organic farming (using natural fertilisers and biological control instead of synthetic chemicals) and hydroponics (growing plants in nutrient solutions without soil, allowing year-round production in controlled environments with less water use than traditional farming).

Key Fact

Tissue culture produces many identical plants from a single parent rapidly. Biological control uses natural predators rather than chemicals. Crop rotation and hydroponics are examples of sustainable farming practices that increase food security.
